title: C346 — Inline connector reference
introduction:
I start with the MALE or FEMALE harness heading, then use the cavity labels in that section's drawing to find the matching table rows. Treat the labels like seat assignments: choose the correct section before deciding where anything belongs. Similar connector outlines are only part of the identification.

Each cavity row links a position to circuit identity, wire details, function and terminal information. This reference includes fuse-or-circuit-breaker-related, active-exhaust-control and ground entries. Compare the halves through Circuit Number, then read each side's Color and Gauge independently. A change in wire appearance across a connection does not by itself mean the circuit identity has changed.

Read shaded positions together with Used and Terminal Part Number, preserving the difference between a blank field, N/A and the blocked marker. The pigtail table then connects service-part records with engineering-shell records; it does not explain every difference between kits sharing a shell.

This is a guide to the reference, with no physical-access, probing, test or replacement procedure. The drawings do not define a physical viewing-direction convention, and the gauge convention and Size and Used codes remain unexplained. Keep those details as printed rather than supplying a guessed meaning.

edits.why: The harness heading identifies which half the drawing represents. In this drawing, the upper-left and lower-right positions are shaded. Use that appearance to navigate the reference alongside the table, without treating shading as a measurement.

Cavity is the bridge from the drawing to the row's circuit and wire information. Notice that the active-exhaust-control row retains circuit details while its Used entry differs from the corresponding female entry. That difference must remain visible; the circuit description alone does not establish a populated connection.

I read the female labels afresh because its layout differs from the male drawing. Its lower-left position is shaded. The drawn positions describe this illustration, not a verified viewing direction for an installed connector.

Read across each female row for its own wire and terminal information, then use circuit identity when comparing it with the male table. Different color or gauge entries should not be silently copied across the connection, and blank entries do not diagnose a failure.

The relationship between Fpn and Engineering Shell helps explain which records belong to the same shell. Several service-part rows can share that shell, so the table alone does not settle kit interchangeability. Keep pigtail gauge information separate from the face-pin wire entries; no replacement-wire or splice instructions are taught here.
